translation:
4. A leech's remedy: for a festering wound, to determine whether it will heal — whether the ailment is in one of the organs, or in the throat, or elsewhere in the body — a salve for this: take a preparation of plants; apply it to the sore; take a swallow of the mixture.
5. A remedy: let the physician take a mouthful of a preparation, rub it about, apply it to the tongue and mouth for soreness; for the same condition, for swelling in the palate: a third remedy.
6. A remedy for toothache: if a worm causes the toothache, and for pain in all the teeth; also for sudden toothache; and for pain in the gums.
7. A remedy if a man vomits blood.
8. A remedy for a swelling: split it and pinch it; apply a poultice, and a good salve.
8. A remedy to stop blood flowing out freely: bind the blood vessel tightly; let it reduce; diminish it; prepare a mixture: combine equal parts.
10. A remedy for a sore joint: if it is inflamed.
11. A remedy for a prolonged illness.
12. A remedy for a shoulder complaint; and a remedy for pain in the kale-stalk [intestines/bowel].

translation:
These are medical remedies.
A remedy for swelling of the veins.
A remedy for woad.
Remedies for a cough, how it comes upon a person's body, and how one should treat it. Three prescriptions for a cough, and for shortness of breath, and then for relieving a cough.
Remedies for chest pain — four prescriptions.
Remedies for throat pain — five prescriptions.
Remedies for the great hiccup, and how it comes about — from a weakened stomach, or from excessive heat, or from too much phlegm, or from a harmful temper, or from eating too much moist food — and how one should treat it, a remedy for each condition.
Remedies for a bloated stomach.
Remedies for shoulder pain — three prescriptions.
Remedies for pain in the side and for pain in the flank — pine prescriptions.
Remedies for linden-tree sickness — a prescription.
Remedies for thigh pain — a prescription, and for knee pain thereafter.

4. Remedies for pain of the joints. Tis penso physic.
5. Remedies for shank disease. For the shanks when the limbs of the shin are swollen, a swelling from humors, a splint may help.
6. Remedies for swelling within. If there is inflammation, if the spell of illness comes, or if many pustules arise, to draw out the matter within, to treat it: this is for that condition — all for swollen joints.
27. Remedies for gout. For the condition of the limbs, of the foot if there is swelling, when it has long lasted, six joints.

For the body, with suppurations, against swellings, a salve:
of preparations, of the same kind, take with all those of the hen,
suppurations in the palate, apply to that part of the body.
XI. Medical remedies for the pale swollen inflammation: take
a bath, of preparations, against pepper-corns, take
warm to the body, and against sores here and there, take sulfur
put on, take a salve of preparations against skin inflammation
take all against swelling. Medical remedies.
VIII. Medical remedies, of preparations, take sulfur, a small amount, against eruptions
of the sores, eight portions of wolf
If suppuration breaks from a dog's wound, take against the nails
take bread thereon.
XVI. Major medical remedies against eruptions, brass applied to the sores,
for the wounds of the body, anoint them with oil,
how one shall treat this: if it breaks open severely,
take the noble remedy, take it every morning, and let one
take the father's blood as one shall require; if one
shall cut a limb from the trunk; or else if
one must cut within the house; take bread of preparations,
take a salve against the swelling, with oil.
XXVI. Medical remedies against skin disease, for each inflammation that is hot.

translation:
Against a festering swelling that is very painful: if a person cannot retain their food, and fails a little, and if they cannot urinate, and if they urinate blood, and if there is danger in those conditions: fourteen remedies.

37. A remedy against when a person cannot retain their food, and if they fail a little, and if they cannot urinate, and if they urinate blood, and if there is danger: fourteen remedies.

38. A remedy for wounds: for a festering swelling, against all wounds, and for each wound on the body, to treat a wound, for a bruise, if there is a swelling in the throat, against a dog's bite, a remedy for lung disease, for an internal wound, a remedy, a half remedy for an inflamed wound, a small wound: if a person is wounded, or struck with a weapon, or beaten with a rod, or if a joint is from a limb, or a snake or a dog has bitten, or if the foot is injured, a remedy for cleansing a wound, a remedy for gathering people together: remedies.

39. Remedies against all kinds of illness, all festering swellings, against conditions coming from outside, against all conditions.

translation:
Against all bleeding of wounds. Against all swelling from heat. Against swelling of glands, against all swellings. Against all swellings, this is the recipe.

40. The physician's remedy: a poultice against all swellings of the joints.

51. The physician's remedy against swelling within the joints.

52. The physician's remedy against dysentery. Boil elder-bark together with it. Against swelling, take elder-bark together; against sore muscles and on the body, strain through a cloth and strain again through a cloth of silk.

53. The physician's remedy against pain in the bowels.

54. The physician's remedy against pain inside, that is against rupture; against that which causes pain. Take this and mix it together.

45. The physician's remedy for all manner of ailments. Against pain in the limbs, against bruising, against soreness, against all manner of bodily suffering that a person has, and if any part of the body is swollen; take juice of elderberry and boil it well. Each day take elderberry boiled down, against all ailments; against swelling throughout, against each of all pains; if the head aches, rub on the scalp; against this let the physician know; and let the man be treated.

If one has pain in the head or temples, take pepper, the dove's feather-soft herbs, rub them finely, put vinegar on the sore with that preparation on both sides, then mix with pepper, or take woad seed, grind it on vinegar, smear well with that, rub it on the neck with it. If this condition has come from great heat, the physician should treat it with cold medicine. If it should be of a cold kind, then the physician should treat it with hot medicine. The physician must take care and mix rightly to restore a man to health. He must take care not to injure him, and not anoint him with bad ointments.

translation:
For swollen throat or for swollen jaw, the vapors rise in the mouth and cause trouble in the throat.

For eye pain, take pepper and bind it inside with a coriander seed, boil it in water, put it on the eye.

For eye salve, take nut, coriander, and wheat grain, grind them to dust, put into a strainer, press through cloth, put then on the eye. For eye soreness, take garlic, a piece of bread crumb, and pepper, pound well in a mortar, bind on the eye at night. For toothache, take pepper and apply; take juice of allheal, the root knob beneath the eye-socket, and apply it.

description: England's oldest medical compendium. Compiled c.950 CE at Winchester. Contains remedies recently found to combat MRSA.
translation:
For throat ailment from the uvula: one should thin the mucous membrane with worm-sliders; take pepper and then pound the herbs, or rub with elderberry; one should drink with wine from a peel; or the greatest remedy — drink with wine or vinegar; against tapeworm or moth-worm, or against ringworm, or against gingipans: sometimes a single one, as prescribed, sometimes the herbs together, put through to drink after peeling. If there is a hot sweat and yellow matter on the stomach, gathered there — draw it out with a cup; heat the drink thinly inside, along the stomach; give him then a lukewarm drink, very hot; put then lard in oil; sing to him often; in a hot bath, so that he may stiffen; give him against throat ailment an old drink and vinegar to drink, and pound appletanin into wine.

XVIIII

If a plaster does not relieve him, or if there is no remedy, or if there is indigestion in the stomach, or if there be a bitter cough — take gall and pepper; drink in warm liquid drinks.

XX.
For shoulder pain: take aloe, spinach, pressed together with elderberries, mix with almonds, for worms take lemon. Also for shoulder pain: take pepper spice, for chest pain take bishop's spice, for bile spice. Also take willow bark, steep in oil, drink often, season with wine spirit. translation: Often: rub above, then up along the neck, wipe away to cleanse the binding on the side. For betony: soak it as for a three-day pressing, take pepper seven times thirty, pound together, stir well, add three portions of wool to the place, anoint the limb, apply with skill. For pain in the side: take southernwood, rub it, bind it around, the physician shall stay in the house to bite it away. For pain in the side: take stalks of colewort, pound the woman, burn to ashes, take elecampane, rub around, wash on the side. XII. For pain in the spine: take a portion of betony, of the pressings of the plant, do bite into it, take fresh ale, of the cup a portion; anoint with great skill. Also take groundsel, rub it, give to drink with skill. For spine pain: take the plant called elecampane, pound it up. For the same: take the herb hound's tongue, take the leaves, cut small, add to melilot, take then brooklime, rub, apply it.

description: England's oldest medical compendium. Compiled c.950 CE at Winchester. Contains remedies recently found to combat MRSA.
translation:
Apply the herb called elecampane, nettles; pour into a bath and bathe with it.     25.
If sinews are torn, take pepper, thorn, hamo-wort, and betony, and hound's-wort, and lin-wort, and pudding-grass, and thistle, and hop-wort; boil in water and smear on.
If a sinew is destroyed, take bone-wort and another herb, and a third, mix them together, and apply to the place.    For a destroyed limb:
Take a poultice and apply over the destroyed limb; wrap it with elm bark; put metal on it; let it sit until the swelling subsides; wrap the elm around it; take the viper; put it on the wound; then take a linen bandage and bind with it; anoint well; that will make it good; apply to the limb.     26.
If a sinew cramps and tightens on a swelling, take fresh water and pour it on; smear it on the nape where it aches. For those whose sinews cramp often, take the same preparation, apply it and smear on, and together mix nettles.

translation:
This herb, when it is called hot, rub along the hamstrings with stone-bath water, then
when it loosens, rub the bones as he
can manage, and say a spell and give vomit on
top — take it by mouth. If sinew swells,
pound the herb and mix with oil,
and lay it on. Take another herb, mix with juice of pine,
boil until reduced, mix together, cut with it — soon
the swelling will be brought down. Twenty-seven.
For gout: brooklime, fennel,
nibban, alpa sinpela — mix with milk,
with this ointment rub the swollen limb on the upper
half — bathe it, apply to the sore place, lay on.
Take then garlic, boil
and lay on. For stomach-sourness or swelling
of the spleen: bake bread steeped thick,
mix with vinegar. For hand wounds:
mix spelge, brew together, mix with fat.
For gout, give pot-herb with spice, pound
the herb — a man should mix it with oil
and anoint. For gout, take horehound.

translation:
Quickly mix with herb juice and apply to the uvula with it.
For a swelling of the throat: take elder leaves, spread around, and mugwort, pound them alike and bind them on.

XXVIII

For bone-ache: tutsan herb, henbane, Paul's herb, old spittle, chewed — pour through a strainer or a goose quill — mix together, lay on it.
For bone-ache: sit in a warm place, take oil, pound with cress, Paul's herb, honey, garlic, then pound together and apply to the sore joint, smear over it — that will ease the pain; wash off with that preparation, dry out — take of tutsan, of polypody, of fungus, of elecampane — do all of these together according to measure.

XXIX

If a man should suffer with a swollen wound that has festered, steep betony in wine — apply the wet cloths and bind them under with it. Then dig up hne-dylfalt or ground-ivy, take savory seed in the preparation — apply it with a large cloth.
Also: dill — bathe with it; mix together against the humors; use the herb as a salve; wash off afterwards — then apply the dressing again.

translation:
Pound with white mustard; if one uses the flour mixture on the swelling, boil it with pepper.

For neck swelling. XXX.
If a calf's pipe becomes inflamed and for the swelling of the neck: take away the flesh from it; gather motherwort, meadowsweet, and agrimony; pound them together into a powder; mix with honey and treat with it.

XXXI.
For every kind of blister or ulcer: take a roasted grain preparation without salt, mix it, and lay the honey on it. Then take linseed flour mixed without need of cold; put it on. Afterwards bind it with a cloth mixed with new oil laid on. For blisters, make a binding, mix with new oil, or take burned horn and mix with that. Afterwards the oil, pressed and blended with goat's milk, will draw out the blister's core. For blisters, take a knife-cut of garlic, pound it with oil, melt with wax and apply; lay it on.
For blisters, take the juice of a plahe-herb mixed, wash the wound clean with the mustard water, smear it upon the blister.

translation:
For this condition. Again take the herb goat's foot, three parts boiled in vinegar. Again for a swelling, with pyrethrum mixed and with flour and with celandine, boiled without mixing. For a wolf-sore, take this herb, scrape the hair from the horn, or it has the power to mingle with the meal, smear it on the swollen part, the honey draws out the evil sore accordingly.
For a swelling, take the herb called garlic, boil in vinegar, let it cool, then add to it crushed peas.
For every kind of wolf-sore, take the plant called lavender, prepared with pyrethrum, ground together, apply to the wound; it helps thereafter. Take also for a foot swelling. For one who is in no way healed, those who are afflicted throughout, or from a rash, or from some ailment of any kind. The plant that is called fleabane. Take it and bind it, apply it frequently to the wound, treat the sores thus, and the wounds likewise. For a swelling, boil it clear.

description: England's oldest medical compendium. Compiled c.950 CE at Winchester. Contains remedies recently found to combat MRSA.
translation:
Take ashes and add to seed, as prepared; lay then upon the boil with a dressing. For a boil: take yolk of egg, grind it together with sifted material and pass through; do this in a vessel; take half a pound of coils of pine, a handful of spume of the sea, work it into a salve.
And if one needs a poultice for a boil: take a quantity of placed herb, thick as honeycomb, lay it over the boil, bind it upon with cloth and over the top do not pull it off. For the swelling: take wax and hemlock, grind them together and work into a paste; bind it upon.
For a painful boil: take a great number of herbs, among them bishop-wort, elecampane, ontre, elehthr, sigson, garlic, mingle together, lay on the boil. For a day-boil: take wound-herb, lay on hot, over the boil, bind with cloth, let it be on overnight. For a boil of long standing: beat thoroughly with wine and salt.

For a hundred sores and similar lesions, take something made from earthworm paste and apply it to the sore. Lay it on the wound in a bed covering, with a remedy of tansy herb.

For a wound remedy: there is an herb called lungwort. When it grows in a stream, where it has no sunshine but lies somewhat in shade underneath the slope, it does not dry out well. Take lungwort, pepper, and the same amount of peppercorns — apply it around the wound. This is a good remedy. A salve of henbane: take a small quantity of old lard and lungwort. It is yellow. Open it up in the middle with a psalm for a man who has a lung wound. A remedy for spider bites: take oil, elecampane, honey. For a wound remedy made with a knife: take the plant called bruisewort, and broad leaves.

O Lord, you who are the father and the son and the holy spirit. All things are under your power. With all things under your governance, we call upon your name; through your word we have been made whole. The serpent was put to flight and the worm driven away; the viper's limb was restored; the harmful thing was extinguished; the snake's bite was healed; nothing noxious remained; the veins were renewed. Still do we call upon you, O Lord, for the life of this creature which comes to us in need of human salvation and relief. You, O Lord, extinguish this poison within the veins, and drive out his venomous creatures and those who afflict him; let there be within you a cleansing evacuation for all whose eyes look to you, that they may hear you, and understand the greatness of your name. And when these things were said, make the sign over him.

Chapter 47.
The physician's remedies against head-wind, brain-wind, elm-wind, ivy-wind, and sundry winds in the roof of the head, and wind in the limbs, hind-loin trouble, and body swellings: wrap the wounds all around, bind them together. Do all this in clear, pure liquid. At least let stand the open wound overnight. In the morning one may then unbind the dressing. Drink it once in the morning, before sunrise, three drinks. At midday, by the power of the remedy prescribed, bid him go boldly; and anoint him; bind his jaws around; and apply drink around. Let it stand a while on him, as much as he may endure. Drink three, nine times, and see that the swelling remains as he wishes. Another remedy against deep wounds: wrap around the limb, sing three times "sursum," make bread upon the joint, set libanos (frankincense) from a mallow. Then take a preparation; take pepper and grind it into a garden herb, and through the liquid sing twelve times; and then be done.

cloth put on up over the knee joints,
not may; often moisten the drink night,
then feel better, be healed thereby.

translation:
For one who wishes to draw out a thorn: take minced pepper, plait it, set it in salt water for three nights, then smear afterward with the preparation given here.

If a worm is in the hand: take the gall of a large fish, add plantain, add dock, and add cleavers; boil up the longwort in that same salt water, simmer them together; smear with it, apply lip salve around it at night, smear with it.

For a swelling from a worm: place the medicine hot against the sore where it is most hot and inflamed.

For a worm in the swelling: some go mad from it, the worm binds the man tightly; some have it in the lungs.

For a worm in the bone: take salt, mix it together, smear with it. Wax salve: for a worm — wax salve, buck's grease, pepper, hot salt, mix together, smear with it.     [Chapter] LI.

If a worm has eaten into a man's flesh, take it to the gall; crush it well with ale, thereupon apply it, take the leaf and pound it down fine.

translation: This is a remedy that is good for a wound. Mix and crush the remedy, and pour it on the wound; apply it to the injury and do not let it hurt. For a swollen wound: take a dog's head, crush it, and then take it and mix with all together. Then take a ripe apple, steep it in water, and press the juice over the apple. For swelling of a wound: take marjoram, mix with water, apply to the wound, and bind it in place. For a sore wound: take tansy, grind it, apply it to the wound, and then smooth it on; also rub it into the wound to aid healing, and say over the wound. For a swollen wound: take vinegar and bark of elder, boil and press it together, and apply it. If pus comes out: take a plant remedy mixed with water and honey, rub it gently together with the hands, apply it. Then take meadowsweet, mix it fine together with honey, and apply until it is healed. If pus comes out, take woad and apply it to the man.

Against pain in all limbs, take this betony dust
and sneezing herbs. Or apply a poultice for swelling.
For pain in the joints and for numbness, mandrake
to drink. For lime-disease, for mood
troubles and fever, aloe, juice of burdock, bishop's wort, liverwort, wall-rue —
take these herbs together and seethe them, with
holy water blessed. Say these words over it.
One should write over a house against disease, and furthermore
over it write with holy water these words:
In principio erat verbum et verbum
erat apud dominum et verbum erat in eum.
Hoc erat: In principio apud dominum omnia
per ipsum facta sunt. And furthermore
go over it with holy water, over the threshold of the house.
Then say the Creed and the Paternoster
last. Recite the Psalm Immaculate before
the Lord as a prayer. Twelve psalms to recite.
A day's prayers are to be said for the bread. In the name of
the Father and Son and of the Holy Spirit.

translation: Or make for him a drink of garlic and holy water, so that he may drink of it every day, and he shall drink it willingly. Sing over it the psalm Beati immaculati, and say Salve me fac over it. Then let him drink it each morning before eating; ring a bell three times and sing for him, saying: Domine, recede, path of all. For broken bones of cattle: costmary, goat's rue, elecampane, brooklime, water-cress, water-horehound, fennel. Let a man sing over the drink or the poultice for bruise or weal, and say the holy prayer. Let him drink it warm at dawn. Each person, in the morning or evening, if they have hiccoughs, let a man recite it and give him good broth. For swollen feet: bishop's wort, oil, bone-wort, crowberry, against the sprite, when it afflicts the creature at dawn. Then let one sing in church the litanies for the holy man, and it shall be done with a girding prayer, and lay about the herb and the potion. Then let him take it and gargle with a swallowing draught. These things: twelve times sing over it, and all who shall drink it shall be cured of whatever affliction befalls them.

For elbow pain and swelling: take linseed, and for throat ailments, for blisters, and for swollen sores — [a charm formula follows] — Boil nettles. A good salve: take bishop's wort, hawthorn, and some meal; pound leek, garlic, and burdock together to make a salve; apply it warm to the top of the head and the brow. Another recipe: take Alexandrian oil, bishop's wort, more of the same, pound leek, agrimony, and clover; rub with holy oil. If a man has a growth, take oil, some leek, brooklime, and halfwort; bind it on.

If blood flows on a thick sticking plaster of linen, provide for it so that there be no harm.
For a leech wound: take the plant and lay it on the injury, crush a leek, put it on, there will be no harm to him. For a gnat or horsefly bite: make a mix of this sort and lay on the wound, and treat it with honey and bind the wound with it. For a hound's bite: take blackthorn bark, heat it in a hot pan, reduce it to dust, and mix with pepper and betony juice and apply on. Put a hound's bite salve on: take the plant preparation, cover the wound with it. For a leech wound: take five plants and apply on the bite, and wrap around outside with a linen bandage fastened with a pin until healed.
Chapter 58
For a mad hound's bite: take agrimony and bryony, mix with honey and apply the preparation on the wound with it. For a hound's wound: take foxglove, pound it, boil it in butter, apply while warm. Then place betony applied upon the bite. Then place bread crumbs upon it. Then apply this additionally.

translation: If the night cramp seizes you — if it troubles you at night, if it pricks you at night, drive it away, all of it — on one's chest from the pressing — let the physician prepare it: if one needs to apply it to any person's body on the sore, without it being forced by necessity, and if the ointment is not needed — and if sometimes within the allotted days it has come back — since this remedy is most powerful when blended together. The Romans, among all southern peoples, had the strongest compound from these ingredients: healing plant pulp, elm-bark, extract — add to it, the physician says: take of bloodwort, of the red one, of the brown one, make it into a powder and dust it. A person should let blood, six cups each, once a month — so then it will take effect. The physician advises: let no man, if within ten nights, or if within nine nights, bleed — if he bled within nine nights or within eight nights, let him not be bled again. Let blood of the six cups each. No bloodletting time is as reliable as on this day — prepare for the palm of the hand and the inside of the arm, and press down into the vein.

If a man's stomach frequently suffers from retching or vomiting, and one cannot stop it easily, and his urine is discolored, then the internal vessels are struck through the blowing, and he will have an uncomfortable feeling of swelling. These ailments come naturally from the flow of blood and from low spirits, and from improper food and various unpleasant aversions within. These will be felt near the region of the heart and in the joints, and in the body's sinews. From all this comes the worst of stomach ailments entering through the vessels. Then one should take these remedies as described, and administer them with a stirring motion into the body, and so it softens.

Here are the signs of a swelling on the lip: the palate, the inside of the lips, and the membrane. The swelling arises from pressure within. There is need for the circulation in the joints to help in the cavity, and the lamb's spleen-meat is effective as a remedy. A red remedy, if your throat is sore: take malt, put it with a little of the bath for the ailing throat. For a Duncan's remedy: take honey, mix it together, give it to Duncan. Have a physician made aware of this, so that it may come to relieve him in his bowl. If the patient's milk-glands are swollen, a swelling arises, and the bladder becomes infected and sore. End. XXXIIII. During the month, seek the Lord of the Psalms, healer of the home, to drive away the enemy. Should there be a swelling of the bladder affecting the heart, he has no relief for it on his own. One should make use of vinegar, mix it with honey, rub on the tongue with the fingers, just a little. A plague remedy for the tongue: anoint it with a preparation.

How one shall heal a person — Chapter 37.

For external treatment, take a mixture of oil and ground herbs and rub it thinly; then lay him down and treat the affected area from outside — massage with the palm, with the fingers, with oil — then apply a poultice. These foods are beneficial: they thin the blood, as long as small birds and all fowl are avoided, for they are of little bodily nourishment and weak substance. Take a preparation of broth and half-healed herbs, infused with honey — rub it in thoroughly. Note: certain foods and drinks are of no use when the bowels are weakened, nor is wine good for him in this condition — it irritates the gut. Chapter 38.

This is for a swollen and deeply inflamed spleen:
take a heated preparation, applied so that it does good
on the hip, and also for the groin, and mix in cress seed and celery,
then have the patient lie on bread, baked or otherwise,
and give him daily this poultice for the spleen.
If there is a swelling or lump in the spleen,
and it cannot then be helped by these things,
for if one finds a collection in the bowels,
if a man has pain on the lower side and it grows,
let the man have a remedy for the sick spleen:
one shall administer vinegar into the deep medicine
that is called oxymelle; those who apply this
shall draw out the disease of the half-side and the disease of the blood.
Take lovage and spearmint and pepper
and southernwood seed, costmary and horehound and evebright:
this will draw out from the man the disease of the gall and the throat-cough.

translation:
Take colne at morning and at night for bruises, drink pepperwort with cold gall of swine. Mix it with lung-wort and drink it. He shall drink the spleen-wort draught, swallow it down so that you swallow it without stopping, as if drawing it in. Bind the bone-splinter, scrape it, wrap a cloth around the knee and the swelling. A remedy for the throat: take gale-wort, boil it on a fire, let it stand overnight, then take the gale-wort and put it into the opening, near the thigh, until it has swollen. Then add salt and season it, mix it and beat it together until dissolved.
For one who has a lung wound: if one has knots on the knee, boil them with butter outside. Another remedy for lung disease: take the leaf of hind-heolop, and the leaf of hind-berry, and the herb gathered near the house and let it be drunk. For lung-disease take hind-berry leaf, and the herb gathered from the hopan. Press it until the wound clears. Then clean with water, boil up all the herbs and drink it. For lung-disease take threel-thorn from the outside, and mix it into mead-wine with mead. Add the herbs. For lung-disease—

translation: For a swelling of the liver: take hollyhock, betony, as much as fits in the fist, southernwood, garlic, herb robert, lavender, and violet. Pound them dry. For difficulty, take equal parts. Then take southernwood, senna, tarragon, on the outside apply paulwort, on a poultice put watercress, this remedy against inner swelling. Apply from above inward. For a disease of the lung: take five handfuls of lavage, dill, and middlewort; grind them to dust; pour over with ale; add pennyroyal repeatedly. And betony, mixed with powder; take a handful of ground material; rub into a salad. This remedy for lung disease: on the inside take marjoram, fine wine, healplant, powder, mixed with pepper and honey. For a disease of the lung again: take southernwood tops, flax flower, henbane, dill, and rue; boil seven parts of pennyroyal; at night apply as a poultice. For all swellings: take the path of the remedy; boil the parts in ale; apply to the limbs; let it draw out the pain for two days. For a swelling of the lung: take black berry-knops.

translation: Open it and give three doses a day: five in the morning, then on the third day nine, then eleven, then thirteen, then fifteen, then seventeen, then nineteen, then twenty-one; then let him drink the rest afterwards thinned. Again, for a lung wound: add to it thinned; let him drink it. For pain in the side: take mouse-wort of the riverside and fennel-wort boiled with birthwort. For lung disease: take betony and oak-rind and ground-ivy, pound together, boil down; take the third part into wheat gruel and let him sup it; afterwards apply birthwort poultice. Again, take liverwort and betony wort, woodruff, pennyroyal, hind-berry, cucumber, centaury, and moss. For lung disease and wound-wort: and moreover, boil wort and meadow-wort in milk. Again, take the dose three times on three days, each portion equal; apply three times; use for three days or nine.

translation: For a scrip drink: take six cups of pine, thirty medicinal herbs, the spartan plant, and moorland plants. Heat them; take the sun's warmth, and juice of the plant, and strip away sinews; make whole the hollow stream, pour it in, and sprinkle with it, and heat it; take the healing, and pour it then to strengthen, to make it ready. And this remedy: take the root of a plant, let it stand so that its strength spreads abroad. And this medicine: take the herb hops, let the plant be crushed, and drink it. If a man needs to be treated, to bring him relief, and his body is being striped with this drink, and the flesh presses and slaps away the soreness: take this drink, elecampane, honey taken in parts, chamomile, a pulp of these herbs, and give a warm drink. Strain it; this hope gives relief when prepared: take this remedy, boil it well, and gather all of the plant together, and take the clean remedy and boil it again, and grind it; and the herb plant draws out soreness across the land; then pour the clear water into it.

translation: Apply this poultice thus: have it stand not too far, wash a bowl full to spit upon, then with honey wash it, set it. Bind it sufficiently warm. Let it stand near the thigh. Drink it in the morning and in the evening, and it will very quickly open widely. Let it remain long standing, and if a man wishes to drink it on an empty stomach, it seems to him a bowl full as though it were drawn out. If it appears to be spreading, grind the poppy herb together for it. It seems to swirl if he wishes. Apply the extracted juice, press out the juices together. It seems to twirl well for him. Let the strips be pressed out, separate the veins together, pound them small, strain them through a cloth to them. Then if the limb is as fair as new cream it is well. Quite well then. Take the roots, eleven handfuls of earth, and hound's tongue herb, pound them all very well together on the outside, prepare them well together. Then also take more, half a measure, or half a pint, mix it with the flour, a handful, mix them together, let them stand near the thigh, set it awhile and this is very good.

Soak it with honey and take a good portion, divide it into small parts. If the person will not take it, take an egg, mix it in ale with a good portion of it, and give it to drink. Rub it thus. translation:
Take samphire, pound it fine, smear it on, press it gently, place it warm on the affected area, let it rest in a vessel of water. For this remedy: samphire, press through with force, dip it on the tongue gently, white portion apply, rub it smooth until it becomes good. Rub it on the affected area in portions, not alone applied, press with a cloth or with a compress, draw out from among what cannot be ground small — that will dissolve it. Do likewise also two times on alternating days, or let it stand. For this condition: if it is good, the remedy works in the morning; if the womb is affected, on the half alternating days, for the human need. Should you need this remedy: the wound, go to nowhere, all the days, do then thirty, apply around, press with moisture, let it dissolve at once. L 1 1 1.
For soreness of the eye: take elecampane from above, bite on bark of aspen, take fine powder of it, lay on the hollow of the eye, take of volonum, grind it, take the fine portion, press against the eye, knead half, take half clear of sediment. For soreness of the eye: pound fine the root of elder.

translation: [A medical remedy:] Take wormwood, ribwort, combed millet in milk with spice. Anoint then, wrap it, take a drink of new wine or pine-apple juice. A light drink for the nerve of the spine: manube, dropwort, milfoil, ground-ivy, betony, water-plantain, hind-plantain, ground-ivy, mint, dill, fennel, earth-bile, drink all steeped. For a swelling of the nerve of the spine: pepper, antidote-herb, spunge, gorse, fennel, [prepare] these boiled together all on a fire, the millet strained off, add no mild drink thereto of nigh a twig measure. Half of that: take a drink of it as preparation. Take it thus as preparation as directed: take oil of aloe poured on, apply it. Smear on the gall of an ox. Apply a poultice to the side. Take herb and hind's hock, pour on ale. Drink it still. Betony, columbine, for a sore mind, anoint with it, with honey, with oil, to relieve pain. Cook until soft, reduce. Recipe LIV:
For swelling in the face: take southernwood, cook it down. Biseleaf, sip the broth, strain through a cloth so no sediment remains. Take it, crush the roots well, add to a drink for the lord's benefit. Apply the dressing with this compress. Recipe LV:
For a man troubled with hoarseness and a cough in the throat: pound together fennel, betony root mixed together. To relieve difficulty swallowing, take a good measure, and fennel seeds roasted, roll small, grind fine, stir into a drink. Take the juice squeezed out, put it in ale or wine, drink it, and do not eat anything sharp for nine days.
For a bath ailment: take biseleaf, betony, groundsel, costmary, pound well together, cook into a drink. Recipe LVI:
If a man cannot urinate: take a handful of common rue and a great measure of mead.

A bowl full of old ale. By these signs one may know the sickness: if a man lies down on his side and his back, that indicates drink until he goes to the physician. Give goat's milk prepared with fennel — give it to drink. Give goat's milk with spelt — give it to drink. Boil a great pan with hops and let it steep well. For a swelling: take elecampane, lay it on the outside of the swelling. Broil elder-wort, grind it in oil.

The signs of disease of the upper intestine and the lower intestine: the illness one may know by these accompanying signs while one is yet alive. If the belly is thin, cleansed with warm liquid, and with certain small crumbs mixed together, and if driven out is filled with matter, and if driven out is bloody — it comes from the upper intestine; or it comes from the lower intestine. If it comes from the upper intestine, this is the prognosis and these are its signs. The physician shall see to it that he speaks his prognosis, and with difficulty and discomfort and movement of the back and bowels — a little blood flows out.

The inner parts and the bowels and the outward passage, and about the joints, nothing at all can relieve it. They are however thus far not bedridden. When the inner parts begin to swell: How a physician must work: a doctor should call for the person to vomit, and take fennel juice, calf broth, white of egg, and vinegar, and boil them together in milk with goat's milk. Let him heat the cheese and not sleep, and cook the following: let him drink pepper in wine. Work it into a poultice, crumbled well, with cinnamon or else cook it with honey, with a mild medicine.

[a remedy number] LXV.
For a horse's chapped skin: Take the hair where it is
affected, then a little lower down, and with three
nights' [treatment]. Then take hops, and the
bark stripped from an elder, as much as will make it bleed. Then
take the sneeze-herb, as much again, mix it so that the
[preparation] serves the stomach's need. If then the pipe/vein is affected or
runs through sinew: For that apply salt. Take
a strip [and] lay it on the back, then the hoof will be healed.
Acquire then the herb-roots, the pond-weed, bind
[it], recite over the preparation: Lord God. For a lame
horse, if it may be helped to recovery: Against the fistula [take]
bel, which grows in the low ground. Take then
from below, pulling upward, [dig] up the root, press
around the sinews of the hand. Mingle a little
[and apply], nine times in the morning. Take
then much mint and pelecinum, boil it [in] new
[milk?], [put it] on the neck, so that the [flesh or wound]
is good, [until it] bleeds fully, [and] heals cleanly, [and] on the
[affected area], cease [giving] him to eat, and [give] him pain relief,
[and] me [i.e., this remedy].

For a wound remedy, take it and apply this, and take a fine skin and press it on the wound, and let blood flow cleanly from the wound of good blood. Soak it in warm water. For a joint remedy, press it upon the limbs, anoint it, press it together. For pain in the joints, take these remedies for the limbs, and for all the joints and muscles, and apply it to the limbs. Then take this and give it to him. Let the leeches press on the joint to draw out the fluid and clean it. Then pour clear liquid over it. For a swelling of the joint, press it in warm poultice. For the sinews, take this good remedy and make it hot: take a good poultice of four sheep's fat and boil it in a pan, and add the herbs. Then for a long sore, bind the hand with a poultice. For a great swelling, press it on the man's limb. Make a good poultice inside: boil it in the juice of herbs and apply it to the pain.

translation:
Take then with the cup after drinking — eight nights, drink a portion. Take lye-water, boil it up with birch-water — eight measures — three parts of pepper, eight measures. Take also pillory and similar plants — add the amount of half a part. Take then where it is painful — cut away the excess. Drink with honey-ale, spiced — say the prayers and blessings for it.

For a swelling in the throat, take at three junctions of the vessels — wash it. For gallbladder trouble, take no portions. Take elecampane, if you have it. At the time the physician prescribes, when you have the means — prepare it: boil at night, the cut pieces and shred — the cuts should be soaked in honey and sliced. Make a boiling at midnight — four cuts, four doses at midnight. Ten cuts, ten doses at midnight. At the next midnight, six, six doses. Take also one cup of pennyroyal. Take an Alexandrian compound — a full dose — add mustard. Drink it in clear ale. It will improve the bad pains of the bladder — a knife's measure. Rub them from above from the roughness — if the throat is rough, it will soon be well. For the restoration of the health of the body, with prayer and devotion — and also with the physician's skill. Take myrrh — cut off your portion — use a good large amount of sheep's wool — doses each night.

translation: This is a remedy for a pustule or wound: it holds healing power and is of benefit against the harm of swellings. When the physician or leech applies this to the same: take a handful each of pennyroyal, savory, sage, and purslane, a handful of each; mince them well together. Take the berries of this plant; let it stand. Remove the tides of mid-morning of Saint John's Eve; take those three days from midday until the tide of the minster. And take the Gospel of Saint John; for those days do not eat at night. For this [remedy] take the following: have a solution prepared; it can be very healing. Apply it with a clean vessel, and bathe with this plant decoction. Then apply a compress for twelve months against all manner of inflamed sores. When the body begins to be affected and the swelling arises, and it becomes blistered, take the berries of this plant and apply to the wound. Remove the swelling and anoint the body in the sun. For an unknown swelling on the body: mince with pennyroyal, a great deal of each; take a sheep's portion thereof, as much as three handfuls.

For land-sickness: reduce the swelling; have oil [illegible] then take a third part rubbed off; anoint with it the whole body and the limbs and joints; truly apply it; then let the physician do so if a man has it. For chilblains: take sloe-bark, elderberry, elm-bark, birch-bark, fennel, young shoots of fern, hare's fur, linden bark, equal measure of each in English: polley, bramble-berry, alder-bark, birch-top, fennel, young shoots, hare's fur, linden bark, equal portions, oil [illegible], linden salve, holy salt, then oil; anoint with it from above until healed. [Chapter] 66.

Concerning famine-sickness, called thus, remedy the eighth:
Take first a drink. Then when you have no peace it will not need to be healed; put it in the sinew with the hand. Then apply the spleen-house plaster; let it not pain inside the wound. Third, take a poison remedy for him.

[For swelling of the stomach, take the plant, put it inside, let it stand for seven nights, strain it through a cloth, do this for thirty days; take a third part of it around thirty nights, mix the remedy, let it be taken for the swelling inside.]

For mist of the eyes: when a man is troubled with discharge and humors, take the juice of celandine and mix together with water inside the eye.

And take of roots, of flowers, of elecampane, of wild celery — mix together with water inside the eye.

For this, take salt, wild garlic, apple, mix into a dust and put on the eye; anoint lightly with wool soaked in pepper milk.

If worms settle in the eye socket, let no man put the plant juice in — the worms will perish and the eye will be healed.

If flesh grows in the eye socket, press firmly, rub it so that it goes away from him.

If the eye grows outward, press it with hot dried dung, with animal blood, or with spittle, or with pepper milk, or with a strong bandage.

Then take the pipe and blow up into the private parts, and rub with both hands in the middle, and press with your hands upon it, and press with your fingers upon the middle. The pain will ease. For a bladder complaint: wormwood, garlic, lovage — boil them together and let the patient drink. Then take a broad loaf. [Chapter] 20.

For a sore in the throat: take radish, liverwort, horehound, camphor, all together, elecampane, geniua herb, oil — give the patient to drink three times a month for three evenings.

translation:
For disease of the spleen, a drink recipe, chapter 26:
Take the plant ele, some plum, take the bark of the elm tree, and fennel, and purslane, and smear with it. Make a brew for the same spleen disease: elecampane, and dwale, and mugwort, and wormwood, and the bark of elder and aspen, and speedwell, and betony. For the same spleen affliction, take hind's tongue, wall germander, bramble, nightshade, agrimony, betony, fennel, dill, and good-all-heal. Drink it fasting for four days, a bowlful. Make a brew for the same: take four measures of hard elecampane, pressed and strained, and take the fine part of the measure, and purslane. Then strain it through, then heat it, and add burning embers with it; mix with the plant and press, squeeze it until it cools. Leave to stand overnight, four times. Take the pressed liquid and put it in a bath. Chapter 27:
For a bruised or injured man: take hind's tongue and boil in water, and give the person to drink; it heals the bruise.

Against inward rotting sore of the throat and sore pain. Take betony, pennyroyal, small hemlock, fennel, and the juice of all. Boil until you have a smooth drink. Take nothing at night except this drink. [Chapter] XXIX.
Against a burn, if a man is scorched with fire on the outer skin: take lily, heliotrope, elecampane, and mix them together. If a man is scorched with a brand and the wound is inward: take lily, poppy, mix them in meal with fine flour for several days. This is for fresh burns: take three cups of butter, mix them fine together. [Chapter] XXX.
Make a good drink for inflammation: take pennyroyal, borage, garlic, pellitory, fennel, tansy, ground elder, and other named herbs. Take three measures of clear ale or diluted ale. Let it stand four nights, press it through; let the patient drink it. Take nothing at night except this drink. Boil and strain through a cloth into a vessel. translation: Of herbs: gall and hyssop gall. Take pan gall, mingle together, smear the wound with the mixture, with the juice; until the pus of the wound runs out, and then it shall not be swollen. Apply the poultice to the wound. Pipe-singing — for the swelling of the throat: throat swelling, ear swelling, cheek swelling, throat swelling, jaw swelling. For each of these swellings take a preparation, boil it until reduced, bathe with the decoction, smear with it; take blossoms, steep them; scrape them, baste; anoint around it, smear with it the heated salve, and blow the salve into the wound; lay the burnt blossoms on it, do so for a day; as long as is needed for the sore to be cured. Take the black salve if the head is sore; take of it twice the measure of a small grain; for swelling inside the throat, for soft swellings, for hard swellings; boil then in vinegar, over a slow fire; strain it off when it is poured out; add the plants and the preparation; it shall be as thick as milk, and as cool; smear it with a feather upon the wound, and apply it over a large portion of the flesh until healed; treat it with honey; press a cloth soaked in it to the wound; apply it again; if it still suppurates further.

For pain of the lungs:
If the throat is very sore, take nettles, gather them, and peony, and libcorn leaf or anise, boil them with some water, and give to drink; for soreness of the lungs. Chapter XLII.

If a person drinks something, and a loathsome thing sticks in the throat, take a bird feather and make a swab, put it into the throat where the thing is stuck, so that he may vomit it forth; if he cannot get it up by himself, and it cannot be brought up by force, use gall. Chapter XLIV.
Against lust, give him a drink of cold water; if he often suffers from uncontrolled desires. Chapter XLV.
If a wound or swelling: take nettles, put them on the wound so that it soon heals. Chapter XLVI.
Take a fine comb, run it through the hair, and take the combings, steep them in water, and give the person to drink if he will. Chapter XLVII.
For lung sickness: if the mouth is foul or painful, take veal, grind it with milk, give it as a poultice.

translation: This is a remedy. Take three pennyworths of cellandine, and pound it; take pith of elder and milk, and bathe with it the affected limb, then bind the cloth around it firmly and wrap it warmly. Press it then with a bandage. And take broom and elm-rind, and ivy-rind, and apuldram-rind, iris-rind, all the plants that grow in marshy ground: heartswort, sinew-wort, elfwort, buttercup, mayweed, betony, agrimony, and scraped bark; pound the roots all together well and blend them. When the sinews shrink and are pulled, give the patient this drink dissolved in warm water, as much as he can take, so that he can move. Bathe him with these bandages and compresses as much as he can endure. When the patient is so afflicted, lay him in bed completely, and let the swellings fly away. Give him a drink of this prescription with warm water, or with warm mead. Give him then a poultice of all these gathered plants, bound about his painful limbs. Wash his head with cold water. Let blood from him every five nights by the waning moon, fourteen or twenty times. Forty-eight.

translation:
Chapter 57

For a swelling in your throat, or a rumbling in the chest, or a swollen uvula: take wild radish, rub it up raw or dried, mix it with butter, and smear it on the swelling; apply the poultice to the throat and let it remain. Chapter 60.

Take a good amount of elderberry juice, the tongue of a bull, and sinew, well ground; add celery, brooklime, leek, and garlic; pound them well together and cook them down in oil until reduced; press out through a cloth and let it stand three nights. Then take the same preparation with the juice of sinew; it shall be good for the tonsils. Chapter 61.

For use as a gargle and for a man who has lost his voice due to disease: take a good quantity of elecampane root, wild celery seed, carrot, bee's wort, harewort, haw berries, black pepper, garlic, leek, hedge berry, grain, gravel root, fennel; pound and boil in water until well reduced; take eight measures, half an apple on birch bark; then strain it and consecrate it with a holy prayer; give it to the sick person divided into portions; keep it a while for the tongue of those who are ill.

description: England's oldest medical compendium. Compiled c.950 CE at Winchester. Contains remedies recently found to combat MRSA.
translation:
Apply these as remedies. For the throat: take cupseed, ponmoho, paysd, and mix with bhge; take oil, eolon, mhse, meal of pancrop, of fine minte, dill, bilir, and tallow; take pollen, mapudir, doece, elltn, petclips, phmod, fomr, beh, xavlaip; take old oil of that mixed with aila; apply the holy remedy of sing-hip to the elder of the shoulder wrapping. So that within no wound of the breast nor bruise, nor wound of puncture, nor wound of hollow channel, nor wound passage should fester, but it should keep itself whole and sound; nor shall pain come upon the man, from it toward peace. Sing their song many times. For three remedies all of them, make now their elder song against wound. LXIIII.
For the relief of young wounds, do apply: take oil of run, fennel, juice, btonice, hind hindolobe; mix together: of fine mead, nise, elen, elfson, pulpsfcomb. Sing twelve times. Of the finest oil it will soon be well. Then after this tasting: take the juice of garlic, oil of it, bishop's purr, pmul, caprule, btonice. Rub the juice, apply to the wound that it may treat it well.

translation:
These remedies for internal [ailment]: a drink for sores within, if there be [illness]: silch — take quinces, sing prayers upon it, apply it.
In thy name give me peace.     Chapter 65.
If there is a condition that has been brought about, to cause the eye to run, to remove [it], as has been said, to anoint around the swelling, if it can help to strengthen [it], to prevent loss of vision, make a preparation: pennyroyal, pellitory, self-heal, a portion of honeysuckle, to find a remedy, then heat the salve, apply with warm milk, each time, put on the poultice five times — cut pieces, having great strength against [infection], each [application] softly — drink, drink, [the preparation] acts upon [the wound], [the healer says]: if a wound is festering inside with old matter or with this pennyroyal, anoint around where it aches, with a preparation of elecampane, let the woman attend to it. If she will not submit to his remedies: make a preparation with galbanum, pennyroyal together, linseed, let it steep, five times, apply a preparation of honeysuckle — if suppuration [occurs], anoint with wheatmeal — if [the wound] seeps, take one piece, anoint, let it soak — if the wound swells up, cut three strips, bind with a bandage on the outside so that it may heal.

translation:
Against chapping, that is striped with cow dung. Chapter 65.
Take and steep it, put it around the hip-joint for pain, beside it, place a bishop's wort unsalted outside, smooth it against the pain upward from below, and bind it with clear water infused with lovage, three masses worth, seven ounces, change it every night; thereafter he shall recover. Take care. Chapter 67.
For swelling of the face: take holy water, say a prayer over it, a bishop's wort, hindheolan, ammonia, alexandrian herb, and ybp-pan pelehi; pound them. Also add: he-goat's gall, fennel knop, garlic, and ground nuts, let it dry. Also smear on the neck from below the chin: handfull of mallow, let it settle, put it in a pan, pour in lollan fully half, and a sound portion. Chapter 70.
For a sore on the body: take a bishop's wort, elder, garlic knop, hindmint, and orache. Let a sound portion hang, and a mild salve, sing over it, say the charm over it, mix it with the juice, put about the wound, cover it, and do not touch it. Say the charm over it twelve masses' worth.

description: England's oldest medical compendium. Compiled c.950 CE at Winchester. Contains remedies recently found to combat MRSA.
translation:
Until one sees that it has run out. Number 68.
Take the plant elecampane, pound it with wine. Take hollow leek leaves,
fill large handfuls and add some ground millet
flour until they are mixed well. Give the patient small
pieces six times a day, four spoonfuls each time, at night
give eight. Let this stand eight nights until the patient recovers.
For one who has an external wound, he is feverish.
Take the seeds of coriander and hyssop, boil them, add fat
and malt. Give the patient juice of pennyroyal to drink
so that soon the pain will depart. Number 70.
Against pain in the belly, take an elecampane drink,
take wormwood, add it to the navel. Apply hot cloths
and the pain of the stomach will be relieved.
If the stomach aches, take this plant greenwort, mix it,
apply it; put it on the chest and anoint the eyes with hot oil.
Against pain in the hands, take old bishop's wort, pound it
and give it to drink. Number 71.
Give fresh water, ground with salt, this mixture blended
together. Apply it. Apply also the balm with a handful
of strong herbs. Take a handful of mugwort. Take a handful,
also a handful of dock.

Thus: he shall take pills — of buckbean, of ahlycep, pour it into from them into hum — take together — and of apple, then of hrepealle, sing (a charm) — in that measure — of the dustup, sing then, nine times — so you put it on — the apple, do so repeatedly, cast off sloe-berry, mixed with it.

XXII
Of vibhcne: take giol-pancoda, gathered at the top, choice — alongside snipping of bean — a nibbing of handful — take a handful — nine times, in the manner of paijo — over the throat-knot — and nine more times, over the tole nan way —
And of celthor-plant, in oil — of Salvia must be pilled — onto spirit-of-bean — [la edenan] — thick and viscous — smear it — and pande — tole nan —
Smear it with human spittle, smear it so that he may find recovery — after relief — the member shall be well — again and again — and then nothing.

XXIII
If it should be that the knee sinew — of the leg — of knees of garlic — and clad and cured of mealcake — put into hands — and add fennel — bone in the sheepfold — with much — of garlic, nine times — of the male nanny — of buccan — so that it be healed — with fish — of the like.
